# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–4 (Complete and Final – Updated 63)

## Setting and Time
- **Period**: Spring through late August of first year; Christmas/New Year period; nearly three weeks into new year (1832) just after Lords threw out Reform Bill; summer and autumn of first year; winter of first year; narrative extends into future years; present day with Fred and Mary at Stone Court in white-haired placidity
- **Primary Locations**: Middlemarch, Lowick, Grange, Freshitt, Mirecombe, Salwick, Quenwick, Fenmere, Bryngate, Chalky Flats, Gulton, Highbury, Cheltenham, Tipton, Yoddrell's farm, Frick, Miremere, Riverston, Quallingham, Halsell Wood, Loamford, Brassing, Stone Court, Coldcombe, St. Peter's Place, Lowick Gate, Shrubs, Dunholt, Yorkshire, Staveton, Bilkley, Harrowgate, Melspring, Wilhaven, Salford; Also: Chiswick Mall (Miss Pinkerton's academy), Hammersmith, Soho, Thames, England, Oxford, Chiswick Church, Buxton, Kensington turnpike, Russell Square, London, Southampton Row, Vauxhall, Exeter 'Change, India (Boggley Wollah, Ramgunge, Budgebudge, Calcutta, Dumdum), Forty Thieves theatre, King's 14th regiment post, Highbury Barn, Covent Garden Market, Doctor Swishtail's Seminary, playground with tree and broken glass on wall, Bedford tavern, Thames Street (City)
- **Current Setting Details**: River crossing at Gulton and Quenwick; forge with chalked crooked sun on wall; wind from water with salt and tar smell; gulls quarreling over fish heads by steps (recurring); smoke from chimneys lying flat over fields; frost silvering hedges overnight; turnip cart passing well; light going early as spring approaches; children chasing hoop down lane; road all ruts and puddles after thaw; market town of Bryngate; hill farms of Coldcombe and Mirecombe; rain threatening but holding off since morning; bees humming in lavender behind parsonage; bell for vespers ringing thinly across roofs; front room on second floor with chintz tent hung round with rich India pattern and double calico of tender rose-colour, featherbed with two pillows; back drawing-room with piano situated in darkness; schoolyard with tree where Arabian Nights may be read in solitude

## Main Characters

**Dorothea and Will Ladislaw (Married)**
- Engaged after Will's return to Middlemarch; now married with infant son; established pattern of two yearly visits to Grange; Dorothea and Will's cousins enjoy playing with visiting children; Sir James never ceased regarding second marriage as mistake; Dorothea's life acts not ideally beautiful but mixed result of young, noble impulse; finely touched spirit with fine issues though not widely visible; full nature spent in channels with no great name; effect incalculably diffusive

**Mary Garth and Fred Garth (Married)**
- Inhabit Stone Court; seen in white-haired placidity at open window; solid mutual happiness; Fred becomes distinguished county farmer; produces work on "Cultivation of Green Crops and the Economy of Cattle-Feeding" winning agricultural meeting congratulations; Fred remains steady, told Mary happiness half owing to Farebrother; never wholly free from misled hopefulness but gradually saved enough to become Stone Court owner; three boys only, youngest resembles grandfather

**Rebecca Sharp (Miss Becky)**
- **Age and Background**: Age nineteen; father was artist/drawing teacher at Miss Pinkerton's academy—clever, prone to debt and tavern, beat wife and daughter when drunk, died after third delirium tremens; mother was French opera-girl; claims descent from noble Entrechats family of Gascony; had dismal precocity of poverty
- **Appearance**: Small, slight, pale, sandy-haired with large, odd, attractive eyes; dressed in white with bare shoulders; white slender fingers
- **Accomplishments**: Speaks French with purity and Parisian accent; skilled musician and linguist; clever artist; sings better than Amelia
- **Departure from Chiswick**: Threw Dixonary at Miss Jemima; obtained governess position with Sir Pitt Crawley's family after months-long battle to cancel indentures; Miss Pinkerton recommended her: "I cannot find fault with Miss Sharp's conduct except to myself; must allow her talents and accomplishments are of high order"; determined to make connected plans for future; never blushed since age eight when caught stealing jam by godmother; capable of calculated charm and intimacy
- **Crisp Affair**: **Rumor claims** tart-woman hinted great deal more than public knowledge regarding Reverend Mr. Crisp's intercepted proposal
- **At Sedley Household**: Invited by Amelia for week before governess duties; won over entire household through charming behavior; laughed at Mr. Sedley's jokes with cordiality; interested Mrs. Blenkinsop in raspberry-jam preserving; called Sambo "Sir" and "Mr. Sambo"; charmed both Drawing Room and Servants' Hall; by day ten on footing of considerable familiarity
- **Regarding Joseph Sedley**: Upon learning of India shawls, determined "If Mr. Joseph Sedley is rich and unmarried, why should I not marry him?"; at dinner made comical air about Arabian Nights and chili; gave Joseph gentle pressure with little hand, drew it back frightened, looked in his face; Joseph's heart thumped
- **Intimate Evening**: Left alone in drawing-room while Amelia and George went to piano; occupied knitting green silk purse; conversation established great confidence and intimacy; Joseph began eloquent speech "O Miss Sharp, how--" but stopped when music ended, blushed, blew nose in agitation
- **Joseph's Feelings Rekindled**: Joseph's heart nestled with Amelia's sweet fresh voice, but Joseph presented nosegays of flowers from Covent Garden Market to both young women; Rebecca said she had never tasted pine and longed beyond everything to taste one; **current state**: Rebecca refuses Joseph's request to sing, citing low spirits; asks him to help finish green silk purse; Joseph seated tete-a-tete looking at her with killing expression, hands bound in web of green silk
- **Joseph's Assessment**: Joseph lay awake thinking of marrying her; concluded "It's evident the poor devil's in love with me"; thought "I might go farther, and fare worse"
- **Observer Assessment**: Osborne caught Miss Sharp's eye fixed keenly upon him, at which he blushed a little, and Rebecca thought in her heart, "Ah, mon beau Monsieur! I think I have YOUR gauge"--the little artful minx!
- **Dinner Talk**: Rebecca kindled with exciting talk of war and glory, Boney and Lord Wellington, the last Gazette; stood to gain if Joseph marries her

**Joseph Sedley**
- **Position and Background**: In East India Company's Civil Service; collector of Boggley Wollah for about eight years; caught liver complaint and returned to Europe; does not live with family but has own lodgings like gay young bachelor
- **Appearance and Habits**: Very stout, puffy man in buckskins and Hessian boots with immense neckcloths, red striped waistcoat, apple green coat with steel buttons; drives horses in Park, dines at fashionable taverns, frequents theatres, appears at opera; extremely talkative in man's society; told several tiger-hunting stories including one about Miss Cutler and Lance the surgeon; helped Rebecca to everything on table, himself gobbled and drank a great deal
- **Indulgences**: Contented himself with bottle of claret besides Madeira at dinner; ate couple plates of strawberries and cream and twenty-four little rout cakes; drank fitting quantity of port-wine tete-a-tete with George Osborne during thunderstorm evening
- **Cowardice**: Nearly cried with vexation at father's joke about ordering elephant from Exeter 'Change
- **Father's Opinion**: Old Mr. Sedley has feeling akin to contempt for son; says Joseph is vain, selfish, lazy, effeminate; cannot endure his airs as man of fashion and laughs heartily at his pompous braggadocio stories; will leave him half his property besides Joseph's own; sure Joseph would say "Good Gad!" and eat dinner as usual if family died; not anxious about him; says "Let him marry whom he likes. It's no affair of mine."
- **Current Situation**: Amelia enthusiastic for match; Joseph been point of saying something very important to Amelia multiple times but cannot unbosom himself of great secret, only rid himself of large sigh and turned away; **expectation**: Every soul in coach agreed that on night of Vauxhall Joseph would propose to make Rebecca Sharp Mrs. Sedley; parents at home acquiesced in arrangement

**Miss Amelia Sedley**
- **Character**: Pupil at Miss Pinkerton's; happy, handsome, seventeen years old; loves Rebecca like sister; natural infirmity of tears; match-maker at heart
- **Betrothal**: Bred up by parents for purpose of marrying George Osborne; banns read in respective families for ten years; appeared to fall in love with George Osborne at single instant when he asked her for music
- **Regarding Rebecca**: Discovered million of virtues in Rebecca; warmed into most tender friendship; shows her rooms, books, piano, dresses, necklaces, braces, laces; insisted Rebecca accept white cornelian and turquoise rings, sprigged muslin, white Cashmere shawl
- **Regarding Joseph's Match**: As young woman of her prudence and temperament, quite enthusiastic for match with Rebecca; compensates with long intimate conversations with Mrs. Blenkinsop, who dropped hints to lady's-maid, who cursorily mentioned to cook, who carried news to tradesmen, so Joseph's marriage now talked of by considerable number in Russell Square world; entirely agrees with mother's changed opinion regarding Joseph's choice

**George Osborne**
- **Background**: Sedley's godson; family friend for twenty-three years; received silver cup at six weeks old; received coral with gold whistle and bells at six months; regularly "tipped" at Christmas; thrashed by Joseph Sedley when hobbadehoy
- **Character and Feelings**: Clever artist; did not seem least disappointed at Vauxhall cancellation; felt extraordinary, almost irresistible impulse to seize Amelia in arms and kiss her; hinted he should like to sit in dark during piano performance; somehow already present at Russell Square when Joseph arrived next morning
- **Betrothal**: Bred up by parents for purpose of marrying Amelia; banns read in respective families for ten years; appeared to fall in love with Amelia at single instant
- **Compliments to Others**: Said of Dobbin "There's not a finer fellow in the service, nor a better officer, though he is not an Adonis, certainly"; at Vauxhall plans spoke of resistance to French Invasion
- **Character Assessment**: Though little chap, had very high popularity among Swishtail youth; said of Dobbin "After all, it's not his fault that his father's a grocer"; his opinion received with great applause; broke punch-bowl at child's party seven years ago
- **Recent Contacts**: Met Dobbin at Bedford tavern and told him Miss Amelia was come home and they were all bent on going out for night's pleasuring

**William Dobbin** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Background**: Son of merchant/grocer; father keeps shop "Figs & Rudge" on Thames Street, City
- **Rise in Social Standing**: Despised grocer became Alderman Dobbin; Alderman Dobbin was Colonel of City Light Horse burning with military ardour to resist French Invasion; Colonel Dobbin's corps reviewed by Sovereign and Duke of York; colonel and alderman knighted; his son entered army; young Osborne followed in same regiment; they served in West Indies and in Canada; their regiment just come home
- **School Experience**: Giant amongst boys at Doctor Swishtail's Seminary, downcast and stupefied appearance, dog's-eared primer, tight corduroys; incapable of acquiring Latin rudiments; continually "taken down" by small boys; mercilessly bullied by entire school; corduroys sewn up, bed-strings cut, buckets and benches upset, parcels of paternal soap and candles sent to him; bore everything patiently, entirely dumb and miserable; called "Figs" as nickname of reproach
- **Defense of George Osborne and Famous Fight**: While reading Arabian Nights under tree, witnessed Cuff beating small boy; sprang up and cried "Hold off, Cuff; don't bully that child any more"; previously threatened Cuff with leaden inkstand, saying "Don't strike, or I'll THMASH you" with such wickedness that Cuff backed down; after that Cuff never meddled personally with Dobbin; young Osborne told Dobbin that Cuff was licking him for breaking milk bottle; Dobbin said "I'll give you the worst thrashing you ever had in your life"; fought thirteen rounds: Cuff initially scientific and contemptuous, floored Dobbin three times; Dobbin quivering and determined, being left-handed brought that arm into action hitting Cuff's left eye and nose; by round 6, as many fellows shouting "Go it, Figs" as "Go it, Cuff"; by round 12, Cuff all abroad, lost presence of mind; round 13 final, Cuff reeling and groggy, Dobbin put in left on nose and sent him down; all boys shouted for Figs; Doctor threatened to flog Dobbin; Cuff acknowledged fault, saved Dobbin from whipping
- **Character Change**: In consequence of victory, character rose prodigiously in estimation; name "Figs" became respectable and popular nickname; "Old Figs" grew to name of kindness and endearment
- **Current Status and Attachment**: Young Osborne wrote home describing fight, telling mother Dobbin licked Cuff, fight was about him, and since Dobbin fought for him she ought to buy Tea and Sugar at his father's; attachment of Dobbin to George Osborne warm and generous now as when two were schoolboys

## Minor Characters and Events
- **Vauxhall Plan**: Thunderstorm on evening appointed prevented attendance; young people remained at home; two gallant young men (Osborne and Dobbin) longed to see their names in glorious list of Gazette victories, cursed unlucky fate to belong to regiment away from chances of honour
- **Mrs. Sedley's Opinion**: Initially thought son would demean himself by marriage with artist's daughter; but Mrs. Blenkinsop recalled "we was only grocers when we married Mr. S., who was a stock-broker's clerk, and we hadn't five hundred pounds among us, and we're rich enough now"; gradually brought to accept match
- **Orlwood and Hollwood Families** [NEW - minor appearances]: Madrek Orlwood fell asleep in chair before fire; Cotho Hollwood shrugged at rain question; Madrek hummed childhood tune while scrubbing step; Fedette Orlwood walked long way round to avoid muddy square; Ilena Orlwood counted coins twice, came up penny short; Madrek spent evening sorting old letters by candlelight; Cotho talked of nothing much—weather, harvest, lame horse; Cotho argued with carter over oats price; Cotho watched clouds and predicted rain wrongly
- **Lindson-Hollmere Blood Debt**: Late one night Fedette Orlwood confided to eldest daughter of Madrek Orlwood that Lindson family once owed blood debt to Hollmere family; Fedette could keep it no longer and told Fetho Hollmere
- **Narrative Frame**: Author notes tune is mild one with terrific chapters coming presently; begs reader remember only discoursing about stockbroker's family in Russell Square taking walks, luncheon, dinner, talking and making love without passionate and wonderful incident; argument stands: Osborne in love with Amelia asked old friend to dinner and Vauxhall; Jos Sedley in love with Rebecca; question is will he marry her
